newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Van Miert hints at full probe of Guinness/GdMet.
newsitem.headline: Van Miert hints at full probe of Guinness/GdMet.

text.p: European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert, scalded by the controversy caused by his comments on the merger betweeen Boeing and McDonnell Douglas, tried hard on Thursday to stay non-committal about new big corporate deals submitted for EU approval.

But under pressure to say something on the merger between drinks groups Guinness Plc and Grand Metropolitan Plc he showed once again that he cannot help speaking his mind -- a frankness that even detractors often admire in him.
Asked at a news conference, called to discuss the liberalisation of the European telecommunications market, to comment on the 23-billion-pound ($37.5 billion) deal, he played safe.
"We have to investigate all the different products related (to the merger)...We are only at the very beginning on this case, so leave us some time to investigate the case properly," he said.

But a second request to comment broke down his defences. Van Miert said he was aware of the competition concerns raised by the deal and, more importantly, dropped an apparent hint that the two companies face an uphill struggle to get the Commission's approval.

"It is well-known, I think, what the problems are, the competition concerns which have been identified. Now the procedure will go ahead, there will be a hearing in a few weeks time and then we will see what comes next," he added.
The problem lies with the word "hearing".

There is no hearing during the preliminary first-month inquiry which in the present case expires on June 20 and antitrust lawyers said it could have been a Freudian slip, showing that Van Miert has already decided that the deal will require a detailed, second-stage probe.
The Commissioner has been criticised for predjudging the issue in the Boeing/McDonnell Douglas case even before the deal was formally submitted for EU approval.

The lawyers said the Belgian Commissioner, who was speaking in English, could just have picked an unfortunate word and that he meant to refer to internal Commission procedures which include meetings with the parties.
The deal was filed for approval on May 16 under EU rules which ban creation or strengthening of dominant positions in the 15-nation bloc.
The Commission must take a decision before June 20 whether to approve it or start a full probe, which could last another four months.
Although the process is still at an early stage, the lawyers said they would not be surprised if the Commission did go to a full probe.
"It would not be in the least a surprise," one said.

The proposed merger gives the Commission a good oportunity to set out its views on the spirits market, which in the EU is still to a certain extent fragmented along national lines due to different tax regimes and distribution traditions.
The deal would bring together brands such as Grand Met's Smirnoff vodka, J&B whisky and Bailey's with Guinness-owned Johnnie Walker and Bell's Scotch whisky and Gordon's gin.
There are only two other large drinks groups in the world besides Guinness and Grand Metropolitan, Allied Domecq and Seagram.

The sources said the European spirits market was slowly declining and there was a danger that the proposed merger would have an impact on small players already having difficulty resisting the power of the big four.
Grand Met's chairman George Bull said early this month when the deal was anounced that he was confident of getting regulatory agreement in both the EU and the United States.
Canada's drinks and entertainment group Seagram has expressed concerns about the new group's strong hold on the world's spirits markets.
